title: "Correlated predictors"

We now return to the [MALD word-item data](multiple-regression.qmd#mald-word-item-data). A partial coefficient compares items that differ in one predictor while holding the others fixed. **Predictor collinearity** arises when the observed design contains relatively few such comparisons because predictor columns move together.

The observed [correlation](../random-variables-and-distributions/correlation.qmd) standardizes covariance between two predictor columns, while multivariable identification depends on residual predictor variation after the other columns are removed. That residualization uses [variance](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd) and the [regression-residual](residuals.qmd) idea algebraically. [Independence](../foundations/independence.qmd) of response rows is a separate likelihood assumption and does not follow from low predictor correlation.

How much partial information remains once the observed predictors move together? We answer by inspecting supported comparisons, coefficient uncertainty, and the limiting case of exact nonidentification.

## Overlap in the MALD item design

Longer spoken words tend to contain more phones and syllables. That empirical relation makes it harder to separate their partial associations with item-mean lexical-decision time.

```{r}
#| label: compute-mald-predictor-correlations
library(ggplot2)

mald <- read.csv("data/mald/mald-items.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
predictor_names <- c(
  "log_frequency_subtlex", "log_duration", "n_phones", "n_syllables"
)
correlation_matrix <- cor(mald[, predictor_names])

stopifnot(
  nrow(mald) == length(unique(mald$item)),
  all(is.finite(correlation_matrix))
)

round(correlation_matrix, 3)
```

Pairwise correlations summarize one projection of the design, but a partial coefficient is identified by multivariable residual variation. The next code finds an observed 25-ms acoustic-duration band with a large phone-count range and displays its shortest- and longest-phone items. These are approximate “similar duration, different phones” comparisons already present in the data.

```{r}
#| label: inspect-mald-partial-support
mald$duration_band_25ms <- 25 * round(mald$duration_ms / 25)
phone_ranges <- vapply(
  split(mald$n_phones, mald$duration_band_25ms),
  function(values) if (length(values) >= 2L) diff(range(values)) else NA_real_,
  numeric(1)
)
support_band <- as.numeric(names(which.max(phone_ranges)))
support_rows <- subset(mald, duration_band_25ms == support_band)
support_rows[c(
  which.min(support_rows$n_phones),
  which.max(support_rows$n_phones)
), c("item", "duration_ms", "n_phones", "n_syllables",
     "frequency_subtlex", "mean_log_rt")]
```

The rows make the partial comparison imaginable, though they do not hold every other predictor exactly fixed. If a fitted coefficient compares combinations far outside the observed joint support, it is an extrapolation even when every individual predictor lies inside its marginal range.

For centered predictor columns $\mathbf x_j$ and $\mathbf x_k$, the sample correlation is

$$
r_{jk}
=
\frac{\mathbf x_j^\top\mathbf x_k}
{\sqrt{(\mathbf x_j^\top\mathbf x_j)
(\mathbf x_k^\top\mathbf x_k)}}.
$$

This normalized inner product is computed from observed MALD item properties. The phone--syllable correlation is `r sprintf("%.3f", correlation_matrix["n_phones", "n_syllables"])`.

```{r}
#| label: plot-mald-correlated-predictors
#| fig-cap: "Observed MALD phone and syllable counts with their fitted item-level relation."
phone_fit <- lm(n_phones ~ n_syllables, data = mald)
grid <- data.frame(n_syllables = sort(unique(mald$n_syllables)))
grid$fitted_phones <- predict(phone_fit, newdata = grid)

point_opacity <- 0.06
ggplot(mald, aes(n_syllables, n_phones)) +
  geom_jitter(
    color = "grey65",
    alpha = point_opacity,
    width = 0.08,
    height = 0.08,
    size = 0.55
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = grid,
    aes(y = fitted_phones),
    color = "#2C6E9B",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  labs(x = "Syllables", y = "Phones") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

If two design columns were exact multiples, $\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X$ would be singular and their separate coefficients would be unidentified. Here the relation is strong but not exact. OLS still returns unique coefficients, though their sampling variances may be inflated.

A potential worry is that correlation makes multiple regression invalid. Correlation alone does not do that. It changes which partial comparisons the design supports and how precisely they can be estimated. The scientific response is to inspect the overlap and align interpretation with it.

Pairwise correlation can also miss multivariable near-dependence, in which one predictor is well approximated by a combination of several others. The auxiliary regressions on the [VIF page](variance-inflation-factors.qmd) inspect that full declared predictor set.

## Recap and check your understanding

1. Which observed item properties overlap most strongly?
2. Why does predictor overlap weaken a partial comparison?
3. What happens under exact linear dependence?
4. Why is a correlated design not automatically unusable?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Phone count and syllable count overlap most strongly in the observed MALD items. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. When predictors move together, few observed items vary in one while holding the other fixed, so the partial coefficient relies on limited comparisons and becomes less precise. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. The design loses rank, $\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf X$ becomes singular, and the separate coefficients are unidentified. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. Imperfect correlation can still leave enough independent variation for unique, scientifically interpretable partial comparisons, though uncertainty may increase. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>

The [next page](variance-inflation-factors.qmd) quantifies the coefficient-variance cost of this overlap.
